Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The general equation of a second order (quadratic) curve is an expression of the form

Content:
[MATH: \alpha_{11}x_1^2+2\alpha_{12}x_1x_2 + \alpha_{22}x_2^2 + 2\alpha_{13}x_1+ 2\alpha_{23}x_2 +\alpha_{33}=0,]

Content:
where [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] are variables, and [MATH: \alpha_{ij} \in \Bbb R] for all [MATH: 1\leq i,j \leq 3.]

Content:
For example,

Content:
[MATH: 3x_1^2-x_1x_2-5x_2^2+5x_2 - 1 = 0]

Content:
is a general quadratic curve.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Non-Degenerate Quadratic Curves

Content:
There are three basic so-called non-degenerate quadratic curves:

Content:
| Standard Equation | Description |
| [MATH: \dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=1] | Ellipse |
| [MATH: \dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=1] | Hyperbola |
| [MATH: x_2^2= 2px_1] | Parabola |

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Degenerate (Real) Quadratic Curves

Content:
There are also a few so-called degenerate (real) quadratic curves:

Content:
| Standard Equation | Description |
| [MATH: \dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0] | Pair of / intersecting lines |
| [MATH: {x_i^2}=a^2] | Pair of / parallel lines |
| [MATH: {x_i^2}=0] | Pair of / coincident lines |
| [MATH: \dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0] | Single point |

Content:
Let's see why these equations define the described curves:

Content:
- [MATH: \dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0] is equivalent to [MATH: (bx_1 - ax_2)(bx_1 + ax_2)=0] which in turn gives equations of two lines [MATH: bx_1 - ax_2=0] and [MATH: bx_1 + ax_2=0] intersecting at the origin.
- [MATH: {x_i^2}=a^2] is equivalent to [MATH: (x_i - a)(x_i + a)=0] which in turn gives equations of two parallel lines [MATH: x_i =a] and [MATH: x_i=-a.]
- [MATH: {x_i^2}=0] gives equations of two coincident lines [MATH: x_i =0] and [MATH: -x_i=0.]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Classifying a General Quadratic Curve

Content:
In general, the cross-term of a quadratic equation can be eliminated by an orthogonal change of variables. That is, one of the kind [MATH: \mathbf{x} =P \mathbf{y} ,] where the columns of [MATH: P] form an orthonormal eigenbasis for the corresponding quadratic form's matrix.

Content:

[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}]]

First, let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

Content:
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}]]

Content:
We know that this change of variables reduces the corresponding quadratic form [MATH: Q(\mathbf x) = 2x_1x_2] to its canonical form. Indeed, performing the change of variables on [MATH: \mathcal C,] gives

Content:
[MATH: 2x_{1}x_{2} − 2sqrt(2)x_{1} + 2sqrt(2)x_{2} = 8⟹y_{1}^{2} − y_{2}^{2} + 4y_{2} = 8,]
and, by completing the square for the variable [MATH: y_2], we get the equation

Content:
[MATH: y_{1}^{2} − (y_{2} − 2)^{2}|= 4.]

Content:
Notice that we can write down the change-of-variables matrix as
[MATH: [(1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2)); (1)/(sqrt(2))|(1)/(sqrt(2))]]
which is a rotation matrix. Looking at the diagram above, we see that going from one coordinate system to another can be viewed as a rotation of our axes by [MATH: 45^\circ.]

Content:
Watch out! In general, this action is an orthogonal transformation (it can be a rotation, a reflection, or a combination of such transformations).

Content:
Finally, performing the change of variables

Content:
[MATH: {z_{1} = y_{1},; z_{2} = y_{2} − 2,]

we get the following:

[MATH: y_{1}^{2} − (y_{2} − 2)^{2}|= 4; (z_{1}^{2})/(4) − (z_{2}^{2})/(4)|= 1; (z_{1}^{2})/(2^{2}) − (z_{2}^{2})/(2^{2})|= 1]
